legend: Luis likes to play with permutations. A permutation is an arrangement of integers such that if its length is N$$$N$$$, then each of its elements is between 1$$$1$$$ and N$$$N$$$, and no element appears more than once. For example, [1,3,4,2]$$$[1,3,4,2]$$$ and [1,2]$$$[1,2]$$$ are permutations, while [1,3,4]$$$[1,3,4]$$$ and [1,2,4,2]$$$[1,2,4,2]$$$ are not. In a permutation P$$$P$$$ of length N$$$N$$$, we denote P[1],P[2],…,P[N]$$${P[1]}, {P[2]}, \ldots, {P[N]}$$$ as its elements in the order they appear in P$$$P$$$. For example, for P=[1,3,4,2]$$$P=[1,3,4,2]$$$, we have P[3]=4$$$P[3]=4$$$.

Luis is interested in the semi-fixed points of permutations. An integer x$$$x$$$ is a semi-fixed point of a permutation P$$$P$$$ if P[P[x]]=x$$$P[P[x]]=x$$$. We denote s(P)$$$s(P)$$$ as the number of semi-fixed points of the permutation P$$$P$$$. For example, for P=[3,6,1,4,2,5]$$$P=[3,6,1,4,2,5]$$$, we have s(P)=3$$$s(P)=3$$$ since 1$$$1$$$, 3$$$3$$$, and 4$$$4$$$ are the semi-fixed points of P$$$P$$$.
input: The first line contains an integer N$$$N$$$ (1≤N≤2⋅105$$$1 \leq N \leq 2 \cdot 10^5$$$) indicating the length of the permutation.
The second line contains N$$$N$$$ distinct integers P[1],P[2],…,P[N]$$${P[1]}, {P[2]}, \ldots, {P[N]}$$$ (1≤P[i]≤N$$$1 \leq P[i] \leq N$$$), the elements of the permutation P$$$P$$$.
output: A line with an integer, the result of the calculation that Luis wants to compute.
note: In the first example, P=[1,3,4,2]$$$P=[1,3,4,2]$$$ and its rotations are:
rot3(P)=[2,1,3,4]$$$\mathop{\mathrm{rot}}\nolimits^3(P) = [2, 1, 3, 4]$$$, with 4$$$4$$$ semi-fixed points, which are 1,2,3$$$1, 2, 3$$$, and 4$$$4$$$.
